sources_considered.why: ARC-AGI-3 scores for frontier models in novel, instruction-free environments.
Primary statement of what ARC-AGI-3 measures.

receipt.public_excerpt: Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro led the pack at 0.37%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 came in at 0.26%. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 managed 0.25%, while xAI’s Grok-4.20 scored exactly zero. Humans, meanwhile, solved 100% of environments.

evidence_items.explanation: Frontier systems scored under 1% where humans scored 100% on tasks requiring self-directed exploration and goal discovery. This is direct evidence of missing flexible, self-directed competence.

receipt.public_excerpt: challenges AI agents to explore novel environments, acquire goals on the fly, build adaptable world models, and learn continuously.

evidence_items.explanation: Shows the benchmark measures flexible, self-directed competence of the kind the claim describes.

evidence_items.locator: section 'Claude 4.6 Opus On METR: The numbers', paragraph 1

receipt.public_excerpt: METR’s latest measurements put Claude Opus 4.6 at a 50%-time horizon of approximately 14.5 hours

evidence_items.explanation: Shows strong, rising capability on well-specified tasks. This is consistent with the claim's concession that systems are powerful and increasingly useful.

evidence_items.publisher: Nature (Comment by Chen, Belkin, Bergen, Danks)

receipt.public_excerpt: The vision of human-level machine intelligence laid out by Alan Turing in the 1950s is now a reality.

evidence_items.explanation: An expert opinion that general intelligence had already been reached. It is an argument, not a measurement, so it is context only.

unresolved_gaps: The decisive benchmark results came about five weeks after the post, though they cover models current at the post.
No agreed operational definition of 'flexible, self-directed competence'.
